#5983. Airport Lounges Just For Singles—A Boarding Pass, A Cover Charge, And A Chance At Finding Love

A traveler wants major airports to open lounges just for single people: pay to get in, meet other singles, and skip the guessing about whether someone wants to be approached. The comments immediately went to (a) married men and (b) Minute Suites. I don’t think the idea is crazy. A boarding pass, TSA screening and lounge access already do some pre-qualifying of potential dates and mates. Add people going to a location where everyone’s signaling they’re open to meeting someone solves the coordination problem. I wonder if it would make more sense to test it inside an existing lounge rather than signing an airport lease for a singles club though. Professional pickleball player Shelby Bates lays out the proposal in an Instagram reel tagged at Atlanta’s airport. She names New York JFK, Atlanta and Los Angeles, proposes an admission fee, and suggests activities, a communal table, speed dating and televisions showing sports (so you already know what team someone likes before making an approach). There needs to be a lounge for single people. A fee to get in. You’re going in there with the mindset that you’re single. Everyone else in there is single. People can approach you, talk to you. She figures she needs to get in touch with an airport CEO. Watch Shelby Bates propose airport lounges for singles But Will The Men Even Be Single Or Just Take Off Their Wedding Bands? Some people love the idea. Others point out that a person can be flying alone without being single, or that the person you meet may live 2,000 miles away – airports are optimizing for long distance relationships. Then there are these: @mauriciopaiz: “Just spent the night in ATL… they should promote the minute suites a bit more 😂” @chinedumikwuakor: “Just gonna be a bunch of married people in that mix lol.” @motobecanegt: “ ‘So, where do you live?’ ‘2000 miles away from you.’ ‘Oooh, we should date.’ ” @mikelyonsphotography: “They are there, it’s called… ‘United Club’.” He then offers to meet her at an airport that weekend. @taliafvr92: “Ugh no!!! I love being single and left alone in the lounge” There’s Already Some Sorting Happening I’ve written about airport lounges and PreCheck as filters for potential dates. A staffed public venue behind security, with cameras and airport police available, has advantages for a first meeting. Travelers have been screened for weapons. Flying and paying for lounge access also let you infer someone’s resources. It’s imperfect information. And a security checkpoint doesn’t get you a full background check (PreCheck is at least going to cover many offenses). Priority Pass would be an interesting addition. If the lounge was accessible that way, it would attract guests whose cards cover their visits. Then the premium credit card it’s attached to serves as a rough signal of creditworthiness (of course Priority Pass also sells memberships directly). The strongest filter would be wanting to meet someone. Earlier this year I wrote about a woman who got an Amex Platinum card to network with rich people in lounges and made “0 connections”. Everyone was eating, scrolling or sleeping. A designated singles space changes that expectation. People still get to decline an approach, and staff would need to deal with anyone who won’t take no for an answer. But you’re no longer trying to work out whether the person beside you wants to talk or finish a presentation. Most lounges might not have enough room, but what about the new 55,000 square foot United Club in Houston? Another benefit is that your flight departure serves as a natural end to that first conversation. Or, if things are going well, missing the flight adds real dramatic tension and a story to tell you grandchildren. People Have Been Trying This For Years Excluding couples and families shrinks the customer base for a lounge. That doesn’t kill the idea if enough people were uniquely motivated by the concept. The operator still needs enough compatible people present at the same time. Age, attraction, orientation, relationship goals and boarding times all winnow down the dating pool. The operator would need rent, buildout cash and a revenue share. They’d cover staffing and food costs. You’re going up against Chase, American Express, Capital One, Airport Dimensions, TAV Services and others bidding for the space. Priority Pass could help supply visits and revenue. But when entry is included with a card, some people will come for the food and drinks and not actually be open to date. People have been trying versions of this for years. In 2015, Lounger proposed matching travelers who had lounge guest privileges with people who wanted to join them. I’ve also covered AirDates, Wingman and the idea of selling introductions through seat assignments. Calls for designated singles lounges were turning up in New York Times airport romance coverage last year. In this reel’s comments, GateF8 showed up to promote its airport connection app. Bates said she’d try it on upcoming trips. I actually think an airport singles event in a lounge would be interesting just for the buzzworthy media coverage it could generate. It may be a collossally bad idea on an ongoing basis but as a one-off it’s surely worth the earned media. People have been trying versions of this for years. In 2015, Lounger proposed matching travelers who had lounge guest privileges with people who wanted to join them. I’ve also covered AirDates, Wingman and the idea of selling introductions through seat assignments. Calls for designated singles lounges were turning up in New York Times airport romance coverage last year.

In this reel’s comments, GateF8 showed up to promote its airport connection app. Bates said she’d try it on upcoming trips. I actually think an airport singles event in a lounge would be interesting just for the buzzworthy media coverage it could generate. It may be a collossally bad idea on an ongoing basis but as a one-off it’s surely worth the earned media.

#5982. Why Boeing 777 Freighter Conversions Are A Stopgap Built On A Shrinking Supply Of Used Jets

The Boeing 777 is helping the global air cargo industry address a growing shortage of large freighters, but the aircraft providing that additional capacity are becoming very difficult to find. As passenger airlines retain their widebody jets for longer and new-build freighters face production and delivery constraints, three conversion programs are competing to turn used 777s into dedicated cargo aircraft. The irony is that the industry's immediate solution depends on an aging aircraft supply that cannot be replenished indefinitely.

For cargo operators, converted 777s offer an attractive way to obtain substantial payload capacity without waiting for a new-generation freighter. However, their fuel consumption, acquisition costs, and remaining service lives raise questions about their long-term commercial viability. With the Airbus A350F approaching entry into service and the 777-8F still in development, the converted 777 looks like a temporary answer to a problem that will require a more permanent solution.

Growing interest in Boeing 777 passenger-to-freighter (P2F) conversions is closely tied to a shortage of available large widebody freighters. Cargo airlines need more capacity, but the transition from existing production programs to next-generation aircraft has created a gap they can't fill immediately. Production constraints, certification delays, and changing emissions requirements have made used passenger aircraft an important source of additional capacity.

The 777-300ER variant is particularly attractive because of its large fuselage, substantial structural capabilities, and established operational history. Originally designed for long-haul passenger services, the aircraft offers the dimensions and performance needed for demanding cargo operations. Converting an existing passenger aircraft also lets operators add capacity without waiting for a completely new aircraft to be manufactured.

However, the supply of suitable aircraft is becoming a major limitation. Passenger airlines are keeping their 777-300ERs in service longer, partly because delays affecting replacement 777X aircraft have disrupted fleet-renewal plans. This means conversion specialists must compete for a relatively small number of aircraft that are young enough, structurally sound, and economically viable to modify. The question is whether the remaining supply can support the ambitions of the companies developing these conversion programs.

Three companies have emerged as the principal players in the 777 conversion market: Israel Aerospace Industries (IAI), Mammoth Freighters, and Kansas Modification Center (KMC). Although all three target the same broad market, their programs involve different 777 variants, engineering approaches, and development schedules. Their progress also illustrates how quickly the industry is trying to expand conversion capacity before suitable passenger aircraft become even harder to source.

IAI was the first to establish a commercial operation with its 777-300ERSF, also known as the Big Twin. The aircraft entered commercial service in September 2025, with operators including Kalitta Air, Fly Meta and Challenge Group. Mammoth Freighters subsequently secured Federal Aviation Aviation (FAA) certification for its 777-200LRMF in April and delivered the first converted aircraft to Jetran on August 21 for DHL Air UK operations. The company is also developing the larger 777-300ERMF. Meanwhile, KMC is pursuing its 777-300ERCF, which uses a distinctive forward cargo-door design intended to reduce structural weight.

Commercial operations since September 2025

Developing a lightweight forward cargo-door solution

These programs are also expanding geographically. In October, IAI, Ascent Aviation Services and World Star Aviation announced the commencement of 777-300ERSF conversions in North America, with the first aircraft arriving at Ascent's Marana facility in Arizona. The site is expected to operate two parallel conversion lines. Mammoth has also expanded into China through a partnership with STAECO, where the first 777-200LR entered conversion last month. A second line is planned for 2027.

These investments show confidence in the converted 777 market, but adding conversion lines does not automatically increase the number of available aircraft. Companies still need to acquire passenger jets, and customers must be willing to pay substantial sums to secure them.

Boeing is pushing hard to get its answer to the new generation of cargo aircraft out of the factory. However, the 777X delays have trapped its promise

The financial appeal of a passenger-to-freighter conversion is straightforward: an operator buys an existing aircraft, modifies its interior and structure, and puts it into cargo service without paying for a brand-new production freighter. However, the purchase price represents only one part of the investment. The aircraft must undergo extensive structural modifications, maintenance inspections, and potentially expensive engine work before it can begin earning revenue.

According to aircraft consultancy IBA, a half-life 777-300ER converted into a freighter can cost approximately $75 million to $80 million, including the aircraft and conversion work. The investment can approach $100 million if the GE90-115 engines require shop visits. These costs are high, particularly when the resulting aircraft retains the operating characteristics of an older passenger jet rather than incorporating the latest generation of engines and aerodynamic improvements. The aircraft must also have sufficient remaining structural life to justify the expenditure.

Fuel consumption becomes particularly important when operators deploy converted freighters on long-distance routes with high utilization. At the TIACA Air Cargo Forum, Airbus freighter-marketing executive Bernard De L'Estoile described conversions as only part of the solution, arguing that fuel burn matters most when converted aircraft operate frequently over long distances,Air Cargo News reported. His comments should be read in the context of Airbus selling a competing new-build freighter, but the underlying economic issue matters regardless of the manufacturer's commercial interests.

The difference becomes clearer when comparing the Mammoth 777-200LRMF with the next-generation alternatives:

A converted 777 can remain attractive on routes where operators need substantial capacity but cannot justify the investment in a new aircraft. Its economics become less convincing when it flies long-haul services almost continuously, where small differences in fuel consumption accumulate over hundreds of operating hours. The commercial sweet spot is consequently likely to be routes with moderate utilization, not the most demanding intercontinental cargo networks. But if converted aircraft aren't the best long-term option for those networks, what will replace them?

The long-term answer lies in purpose-built freighters designed around modern engines, improved aerodynamics, and dedicated cargo operations. Airbus and Boeing are both developing aircraft to replace older widebody freighters, but their delivery schedules mean converted 777s will remain relevant during the transition. The A350F is currently further along in its development program, while the 777-8F is expected to arrive later in the decade.

Airbus achieved a major milestone on September 29, when the A350F completed its maiden flight. The aircraft flew for four hours and 10 minutes, beginning a flight-test campaign expected to last more than nine months. Airbus is targeting initial deliveries in the second half of 2027, although some industry observers believe the program could slip into 2028. The manufacturer had secured 115 firm orders from 14 disclosed customers by the end of August. The A350F offers a maximum structural payload of 111 tonnes and a range of 4,700 nautical miles, with Rolls-Royce Trent XWB-97 engines.

Boeing's competing 777-8F is designed to carry even more cargo, with a maximum structural payload of approximately 118.2 tonnes and a range of 5,000 nautical miles. Based on the 777X family, it incorporates a composite wing and GE9X engines, offering improved efficiency compared with the current-generation 777F. Boeing also advertises 17% more cargo volume than the existing 777F. However, the program has experienced delays, and the manufacturer is targeting deliveries around 2029, approximately two years after the expected first delivery of the 777-9. Boeing had 81 firm 777-8F orders according to the October industry comparison.

The transition will not happen overnight. Even after the first A350Fs and 777-8Fs enter service, production will need time to ramp up, and operators will need time to integrate the aircraft into their networks. That is why converted 777s have an important window to generate revenue, but the length of that window depends on whether the new-build programs meet their delivery commitments. Another complication is that the existing 777F production line has received additional time, potentially changing conversion demand.

Cargo flats are getting older, and the end is getting further out of sight. With delays more common than ever, when will cargo operators modernize?

Passenger-aircraft availability is becoming the biggest constraint on the conversion market. Strong demand for the Boeing 777-300ER has kept residual values relatively high, while 777X delays have encouraged passenger airlines to retain their existing widebody fleets. Some carriers have even invested in additional cabin refurbishments rather than retiring aircraft they originally expected to replace.

This situation creates competition between passenger airlines and freighter conversion companies. A 777-300ER that remains commercially useful in passenger service may generate more value for its existing operator than selling it to a lessor or conversion specialist. The aircraft's age is not necessarily a reason for retirement, particularly when replacement capacity is unavailable. As a result, conversion companies cannot simply purchase as many aircraft as their production facilities can accommodate. They must wait for suitable jets to become available and compete with other buyers.

Boeing is also developing its own freighter production strategy. The FAA granted Boeing an exemption allowing up to 35 additional 777Fs to receive their first airworthiness certificates between January 1, 2028, and January 1, 2031. This provides a temporary extension to the existing production program while operators await the 777-8F. According to Cirium's October 2026 analysis, the extension could influence conversion demand because some customers were waiting for clarity on continued factory-built 777F availability before making purchasing decisions.

However, the waiver does not eliminate the feedstock problem. Cirium reported 86 firm orders across the IAI, Mammoth and KMC conversion programs, while noting that securing individual aircraft for all those commitments remains challenging. The additional 777F production also represents a limited extension, not an unlimited source of new capacity.

The implications are significant for lessors and operators. If used 777 prices continue to rise, conversion costs could exceed what customers are willing to pay, especially when engine maintenance is included. Meanwhile, the A350F and 777-8F will eventually offer more attractive operating economics for airlines flying intensive long-haul networks. The remaining question is whether conversion specialists can deliver enough aircraft before feedstock scarcity and new-build competition make further expansion increasingly difficult.

The 777 conversion market is entering a period in which demand alone will not determine its success. Cargo operators still need large widebody aircraft, and converting existing passenger jets can remain economically attractive in specific markets. However, the availability of suitable airframes, the cost of engine maintenance and the operating efficiency of older aircraft will increasingly determine which conversion programs can remain competitive. The industry is facing a rather unusual situation: it needs more converted 777s, but the aircraft required to produce them are becoming more valuable to their existing owners.

Upcoming milestones include the A350F's anticipated first deliveries in the second half of 2027 and the 777-8F's expected arrival around 2029. In the meantime, IAI, Mammoth Freighters and KMC will need to secure additional passenger aircraft while managing conversion costs and production schedules. The FAA's allowance for 35 additional 777Fs also gives cargo operators another option during the transition, potentially moderating demand for converted aircraft.

Converted 777s will remain an important part of the global freighter market, but they are unlikely to be the industry's permanent answer to the shortage of large cargo aircraft. Their greatest value may lie in connecting two generations of freighters, providing capacity while manufacturers work through development and production challenges. Whether this bridge can be extended will depend less on how many conversion facilities open and more on how many suitable passenger 777s are available for conversion.

#5980. Which Airlines Fly To The Most Countries? One Carrier Has A Huge Lead

I don’t want to bury the lede — in posts, I often reference how Turkish Airlines flies to more countries than any other airline in the world. However, how many countries does the airline actually fly to, and how far ahead of competitors is Turkish Airlines? I thought that would be interesting to explore…

Turkish Airlines has the record for flying to more countries than any other airline in the world. That has been the case for a long time, and in late 2024, the Star Alliance carrier made it official, with a Guinness World Record in the category of “most countries flown to by an airline.” The airline has flown to more countries than any other airline since 2012, and has a sizable lead over competitors.

Just how many countries does Turkish Airlines fly to? This is where it always gets tricky as to what you count. If you count active flights operating at the moment, the airline flies to 117 countries. However:

As you’d expect, when you’re an airline serving virtually every corner of the globe, there will always be some suspended services due to geopolitical factors, etc. What’s cool is that Turkish Airlines is also far from done with its expansion, as the airline still has big growth plans. It’ll be fascinating to see just how many countries the airline eventually serves.

What’s perhaps most impressive about Turkish Airlines’ record for serving the most countries is just how far ahead of competitors the airline is. Turkish Airlines is 30+ countries ahead of the next airline when it comes to countries served.

Does anyone want to take a guess as to which airlines are next on the list? Here are a few general thoughts that come to mind:

With that in mind, which airlines serve the most countries, aside from Turkish Airlines? According to flightconnections.com, here are some observations:

As you can see, that means Qatar Airways serves the most countries after Turkish Airlines, while Air France, British Airways, and Ethiopian Airlines, are currently tied for third place.

Meanwhile it’s impressive that Emirates serves so many countries when you consider that the airline just flies wide body jets. If you combined the networks of Emirates and flydubai (both are owned by the government, but the airlines are run separately), then the combined airline would have close to as many destinations as Turkish Airlines.

Let me of course also acknowledge that the number of countries served and number of destinations served is very different, and US carriers would do much better by the latter metric. And if the question is the number of premium destinations served, then there’s only one right answer. 😉

When you put it all together, below is the chart with the 13 most “global” airlines, in terms of countries served (I had to include KLM as well, since it ties Air Canada and Delta, even if it doesn’t lead the way among European carriers).

Turkish Airlines sets the world record for serving the most countries in the world. The airline actively flies to 117 countries, but including suspended routes, serves 130+ countries. That puts the airline way ahead of the next carriers by this metric, which include Qatar Airways at 86 countries, followed by a tie between Air France, British Airways, and Ethiopian Airlines, at 80 countries.

Are you surprised by the airlines serving the most countries?

#5979. Air France Jet Turns Toward American Airlines Plane After Takeoff At LAX—Controller Warns ‘Traffic 12 O’Clock’

An Air France Airbus A350 turned left toward an American Airlines jet after takeoff from LAX early Saturday morning, requiring urgent intervention. The controller ordered Air France to turn immediately, and told American to return to 2,000 feet. He warned: “Traffic twelve o’clock. Less than a mile.” The incident is strikingly similar to another close call at the same airport almost exactly a year earlier. Air France Turned Toward The American Plane Both flights took off around 12:15 a.m. on November 7: Air France flight 28, an Airbus A350-900 registered F-HUVK, was departing runway 24L for Papeete, Tahiti. American Airlines flight 1660, an Airbus A321 registered N191UW, was departing runway 25R for Dallas–Fort Worth. These are parallel runways on opposite sides of the airport. Air France was supposed to head west over the ocean, but it began turning left – toward the departure path from the southern runway complex. Controller audio and flight tracking replay “Air France zero two eight heavy. Fly heading of two seven zero immediately.” That means turn west, to a compass heading of 270 degrees. Here’s the warning to American: “Traffic twelve o’clock. Less than a mile. Maintain two thousand.” American had already climbed above the altitude the controller wanted it to hold. The controller had to turn Air France away while bringing American back down to 2,000 feet. The FAA departure instructions in effect that day direct aircraft leaving runway 24L to begin on a heading of 251 degrees, proceed DLREY followed by ENNEY. The route continues broadly west. The Air France A350 shouldn’t have made an early left turn into the other departure stream. The controller had told Air France to “climb via” its assigned departure. That means following the published route and its altitude restrictions. He challenged the crew about turning to a heading, and repeatedly asked which departure they’d been instructed to fly. “Air France zero two eight heavy. Thank you very much. Possible pilot deviation. I have a number for you to call when you’re ready.” Air France flew a turn that didn’t match its assigned departure, and it’s not clear yet what happened: a wrong route loaded into the flight computer? a manually selected heading? a misunderstanding in the cockpit? How Close Was This? Simple Flying emphasizes 400 feet of vertical separation. But there was nearly a mile between the two planes. This was serious. Two departing aircraft had converging paths, the controller issued a traffic alert, and ordered an immediate turn while restricting the other aircraft’s altitude. But they didn’t come within 400 feet of colliding. I haven’t seen it reported that there was a collision avoidance resolution advisory. The departure route wasn’t followed, and the cockpit checksprevent the deviation from developing into a traffic conflict. The controller saw the conflict, issued instructions to prevent a problem, and both crews followed those instructions. Almost The Same Thing Happened Last Year On October 31, 2025, an ITA Airways Airbus A330neo departing Los Angeles for Rome turned left toward an American Airlines Airbus A321 bound for New York. It was the same pair of runways with ITA departing 24L, and American departing 25R. The controller ordered ITA right to heading 270 and told American to stop its climb at 1,500 feet. ITA’s crew also received a possible pilot deviation notification. There was also the December 2025 Houston encounter between Volaris El Salvador and a United Express regional jet. In that case, the Volaris crew read back a left turn correctly but turned right, toward the other departure. The United Express crew reported a collision avoidance advisory. I was reading about this incident on X and I found your blog by searching for this specific phrase: ““Fly heading of two seven zero immediately.”

As a non-native English speaker I found myself often struggling very much to understand air traffic controllers (in media, luckily I do not fly myself) because the radio communications are often unclear but also the phraseology is quite specific. What was this instruction supposed to mean? Doesn’t “fly heading of X” mean that pilot should turn X?

Again, not a pilot and not a native speaker, so excuse my ignorance please. Everyone in the thread was piling on the French pilot but a couple of people did bring this up, which made me search for an answer.

This keeps happening at LAX, different carriers, not great. It’s no longer merely a coincidence or ‘distracted pilots’… something isn’t right, and they need to address and resolve it.

Albert – no. Just no. Here are some crayons. Go color or something. Let the adults deal with this.

LAX has, on average, about 800 daily departures, or in excess of 290,000 takeoffs per year. Within the past five years, there have been FOUR highly-publicized incidents of a crew turning the wrong direction immediately after taking off in LAX. So it’s happening roughly 0.00137% of the time. Your idea is ludicrous to put it kindly.

As someone who’s flown into and out of LAX for decades, the problem almost always comes down to a pilot error. If you expect to depart runway 25R, and you set up the “box” (the FMS computer) for it, the route it “grabs” includes the early left turn used by 25R. Now, during taxi out, ATC gives you runway 24L for departure.

Every plane is a little different, but if you follow the correct, prescribed steps in the correct order needed – as you make the changes, the box will grab the associated route with 24L, and give you a course that’s nearly straight ahead instead – as it’s supposed to do. But if you short-cut the steps (just swap the runway, instead of reloading the departure procedure too) and it’s possible to get the 25R route with the 24L runway. That’s likely what happened here. The flight management computer will direct the southbound turn from the northern set of runways.

It is a mistake that becomes likely when a crew is 1) tired (long-haul flying is fatiguing by its very nature, even at the beginning of a flight), 2) tasked with a higher workload because they now must obtain new takeoff data because they got a different runway, and 3) faced increasing workload-management issues as they now received taxi instructions contrary to what they expected… as they are going to a new runway. Heads go “down” (one works on the box and the data, while the other makes sure to follow the correct taxi instructions), cross checking can get missed, and an error can be made.

The solution? No – it’s not to cut 75% of the system. That would make things LESS safe by reducing proficiency and experience. The industry would become less attractive, so fewer would aspire to it. The airline’s new pilot candidate aptitude would drop. Resources to improve safety would evaporate (which created, over the past few decades: GPWS, TCAS, CPDLC, vastly improved on-board weather radar, safety management programs, etc. etc. etc.). The solution is to continue to invest in pilot and ATC training. To insist on two pilots in the flight deck, and adequate training and staffing for ATC.

No aviation system can 100% eliminate all threats, errors, and mistakes (short of just grounding all flights, paving over all airports, and scrapping every plane in existence). What Albert doesn’t seem to realize is what we saw here was the system WORKING. When a mistake happens by one airline crew (the Air France flight) ATC was paying attention, and had the situational awareness to quickly address it. And the American crew was also trained, ready, and capable of quickly handling a non-routine instruction to get out of the way.

When mistakes happen – and they always will – the system needs to quickly catch it and provide a correction before things turn disastrous. That’s how it’s supposed to work, and that is exactly what it did.

PilotPaul – Lindbergh did OK whilst flying solo and without a FMS computer , because he did one take-off at a time . The problem here is too many take-offs and landings at one time .

This is not the elevated experience that LAX’s guests are accustomed to.

So you are equating a rickety, slow, experimental flight that took 33+ hours to complete – that same close to failure on several occasions during the flight (including the takeoff) – as the standard we should strive to duplicate?

PilotPaul – Lindbergh would not have allowed helicopters to cross flight paths at DCA . Lindbergh’s answer would be to reduce them and get a handle on it .

After a six-year hiatus, American Airlines’ most exclusive lounge offering at Los Angeles International Airport (LAX) is back in business.

This week, the carrier reopened Flagship Dining at LAX. That’s American’s a la carte restaurant-style experience, which is available to customers flying in its most premium seats.

It had been closed since 2020 but is now open again after a face-lift.

And it also has a new access policy at LAX — and at the two other American hubs that offer the service.

American now offers Flagship Dining at three of its hubs:

At those airports, you'll find the a la carte dining experience is available within its Flagship Lounge, AA's premium lounge that's open to premium cabin passengers and AAdvantage elites taking long-haul flights.

Instead of grabbing food at the buffet, Flagship Dining offers flyers a sit-down meal with table service — we’re talking a full menu with coursed-out dishes, all complimentary.

In the past, the airline limited access to Flagship Dining to passengers flying in its Flagship First cabin on the Boeing 777-300ER or Airbus A321T aircraft.

But as the carrier gets set to phase out its international-style first-class cabin, access to Flagship Dining is opening up to more passengers.

In September, American began allowing passengers in its Flagship business-class cabins to sit for its exclusive dining experience.

If you’re flying out of DFW, MIA or LAX, you can have a Flagship Dining meal if you are:

That change is especially notable at LAX, because it allows business-class passengers to use Flagship Dining on certain transcontinental flights. To get in, you'll need to have a ticket that's marketed as "Flagship" (domestic first-class tickets won't be enough).

Like with any restaurant or airport lounge, space is limited. You can join the waitlist for a table after arriving at the Flagship Lounge in LA, Dallas and Miami.

American used to offer Flagship Dining at John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK). Today, the carrier instead operates its three premium lounges (Greenwich, Chelsea and Soho) in Terminal 8 with partner British Airways.

Meanwhile, its newest Flagship Lounge at Philadelphia International Airport (PHL) features a la carte dining within the main club.

Speaking of American’s “Flagship” product, the end is rapidly approaching for Flagship First.

Nov. 19 will mark the last date AA offers long-haul first-class as a stand-alone product on its 777s.

Those jets are getting refreshed with new interiors, with the airline ditching first-class and adding the highest business-class seat count it's ever offered.

American will phase out Flagship First on transcontinental service in March.

#5977. Confused Air France Pilots Make Wrong Turn After Takeoff From LAX, Leading To Close Call

An Air France Airbus A350 departing from Los Angeles International Airport (LAX) made a wrong turn after takeoff, sending the plane dangerously close to the path of an American Airlines Airbus A321. The way the pilots responded to this isn’t exactly great, though one thing is for sure — there seems to be a recurring problem involving runway 24L departures from the airport, whatever the cause may be.

YouTube channel You can see ATC has the audio and a visualization of an incident that happened shortly after 12AM on Saturday, November 7, 2026. It involves Air France flight AF28, which was operating to Papeete, French Polynesia (PPT).

LAX has four parallel runways, and the Air France A350 was cleared for takeoff on runway 24L, on the north side of the field. The Air France pilots were instructed to initially fly to the DLREY fix, instructions which they correctly read back.

Once through the DLREY fix, they were instructed to climb via their assigned SID (that they had received with clearance), but then the pilots suddenly made a turn to the left. The issue is that an American A321 had been cleared for takeoff on runway 25R just moments earlier, and that’s to the south of runway 24L.

So when the Air France pilots started turning to the left, they went directly into the path of the American plane. Fortunately the air traffic controller quickly caught this, but it created a traffic alert, and the planes had less than a mile of separation.

Mistakes happen, but what’s strange here is how this was handled after the initial incident. The air traffic controller asked the Air France pilots why they made a turn. The Air France pilot responded “standby,” which is fair enough. Pilots are supposed to be focused first on aviating, then on navigating, and then on communicating.

Moments later, the air traffic controller followed up and asked what departure the pilots had been instructed to fly. Once again, the pilot responded “standby one.” I do think the air traffic controller should’ve been a bit more patient here when a pilot is asking him to hold on for a second. At the same, the Air France pilots seemingly just kept stalling, and seemed to be unable to answer the question.

Of course we don’t know what was going on in the cockpit (it’s possible they were dealing with something else), but the controller wasn’t asking a complicated question. The pilots ended up getting a phone number for a possible pilot deviation.

It’s truly a mystery what caused the pilots to make that left turn, especially since they were flying to Tahiti, which is basically a straight westbound departure (and in the middle of the night, it’s not like you typically need to vector to the east when departing LAX).

Regardless of how good a system looks on paper, you of course have to consider human factors, and how systems are actually perceived. For reasons that are somewhat of a mystery, there seem to be repeated issues with planes departing from runway 24L at LAX making a turn to the left, and turning into the path of planes departing from runway 25R.

Just a couple of weeks ago, I covered how a TAP Air Portugal Airbus A330neo departing runway 24L at LAX made an unauthorized left turn immediately after takeoff, putting itself in the path of another jet.

Heck, just a couple of months ago, an Air France Boeing 777 departing runway 24L at LAX made an almost identical mistake, and turned left right after takeoff, when it wasn’t supposed to.

That’s only the tip of the iceberg in terms of the number of these incidents we’ve seen. I’m not sure what exactly is going on here, and if it’s a case of pilots programming their computers for a departure from runway 25R, only to get assigned runway 24L, or what.

But either way, it seems something should be done here. As redundant as it might sound when you’re sending pilots to a specific fix (which already tells them which direction they should go), it almost seems like air traffic control needs to add in a warning about not making a left turn without authorization. I mean, it sounds silly, but…

An Air France Airbus A350 departing LAX made an unauthorized left turn after takeoff, sending it right into the path of a departing American Airbus A321. The pilots really seemed to struggle with answering air traffic control’s basic questions, though I don’t know what was actually going on in the cockpit.

What’s so strange is how there seem to be repeated issues with departures from runway 24L, as we’ve now seen this “unauthorized left turn” situation from this exact runway several times in recent weeks alone.

What do you make of this LAX runway 24L issue?

#5975. Marriott Bonvoy Boundless Card Review: Worth The $95 Fee For The Free Night

Marriott has co-branded credit cards issued by both American Express and Chase, and it can be tough to figure out the differences between these cards. This is my review of the most popular mid-range Marriott credit card in that portfolio, the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card. It’s a card that many Marriott guests will likely want to have, if eligible.

Let’s dive into the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless Card’s details to see whether it’s worth it and who it makes the most sense for.

Link: Learn more about the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card

Before I get into my full Marriott Bonvoy Boundless Card review, here’s a brief look at the card’s key details:

I also put together my list of pros and cons for the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless Card:

To start, let’s take a look at the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless Card welcome bonus, card eligibility rules, and fees. After all, these are important factors that cardmembers consider when applying for cards. Now is an especially good time to apply, thanks to the current offer.

The Marriott Bonvoy Boundless Card is currently offering a multi-part welcome offer, whereby you can earn three free night awards. The bonus is broken down as follows:

Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Bonvoy points to be worth 0.7 cents each, given all the great ways there are to redeem them. While the maximum value of this offer is 150,000 points, I wouldn’t value the bonus quite that high, given the limited flexibility (you need to redeem the free night award within a year, you’re capped at properties costing 50,000 points, etc.).

However, if it were worth 150,000 points, I’d consider that to have a value of $1,050, and that doesn’t factor in the potential airline statement credits.

If you’re applying for the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless Card, the general Chase application restrictions apply. There aren’t too many direct, consistent rules, but considerations include Chase’s 5/24 rule (which isn’t always enforced), being able to get up to two Chase cards every 30 days, etc.

Beyond that, since both American Express and Chase issue cards for Marriott, there are some pretty complicated restrictions regarding eligibility for this card, so see this post for more details.

To summarize the very basics, you can’t get the welcome bonus on the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless Card if:

The Marriott Bonvoy Boundless Card has a $95 annual fee. You can add authorized users at no extra cost. That’s an incredibly reasonable annual fee, given the amount of annual fee inflation we’ve seen over the years on other cards.

The Bonvoy Boundless Card has no foreign transaction fees, so it’s an excellent card for purchases abroad. That means you can earn rewards on your foreign spending, without having to pay any fees that will offset those rewards. In particular, it’s a good card to use for foreign Marriott spending.

While I wouldn’t recommend using the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless Card for your everyday spending, there are potentially some situations where it could make sense. Let’s go over the rewards structure of the card, including the bonus categories and other incentives to spend.

The Marriott Bonvoy Boundless Card offers 6x Bonvoy points for spending at Marriott-family hotels globally. For many people, this will be a worthwhile bonus.

Since I value Bonvoy points at 0.7 cents each, that’s the equivalent of a 4.2% return on hotel spending. While there are other great cards for hotel spending, some people will want to use this as their card for Marriott spending.

Keep in mind this is on top of the standard points that you can earn for Marriott Bonvoy hotel stays. At most brands, Bonvoy members earn 10x points per dollar spent, and that’s before elite bonuses, which range from 10-75%. So as a Bonvoy Silver member paying with the card (the minimum status you get with this card), you’re looking at earning 17x points per dollar spent at most brands, minimum.

The Marriott Bonvoy Boundless Card offers 3x Bonvoy points on dining, gas station, and grocery store purchases globally. This only applies to the first $6,000 spent on combined purchases in those categories annually, and after that, you’ll earn 2x Bonvoy points on those purchases.

Since I value Bonvoy points at 0.7 cents each, the 3x points is like the equivalent of a 2.1% return on eligible gas, grocery, and dining spending. While there are still more rewarding cards for spending in the categories of dining, gas stations, and groceries, this is about as good of a rewards structure as you’ll see on a Bonvoy credit card.

The Bonvoy Boundless Card offers 2x Bonvoy points on all other eligible purchases. I don’t consider 2x points per dollar spent to be especially compelling since I value that at a return of 1.4 cents per dollar of spending, and there are better cards for everyday spending.

How would I approach the value of Marriott points? As mentioned above, based on my valuations, I consider Bonvoy points to be worth 0.7 cents each. I’m not going to suggest that Bonvoy points are my favorite points currency — they’re not — but the reality is that Marriott has a huge global portfolio, and many of the properties are quite decent.

Generally you’ll find that Bonvoy award stays cost anywhere from 10,000 to 200,000 points per night, though some hotels do fall outside of that range. You can maximize value by taking advantage of the fifth night free benefit, which is open to elite members.

This is an extreme example of value, but take Hotel Cala di Volpe, a Marriott Luxury Collection hotel in Sardinia, which is the brand’s most expensive property in summer. I just pulled up a five night redemption (including a fifth night free) for 776,000 Bonvoy points. By my valuation, that’s like $5,432 worth of points.

Meanwhile the cash rate at the hotel is 4,161 EUR ($4,639) per night, so those same five nights would cost you $23,195. Talk about huge savings!

One unique thing about Bonvoy points is they can also fairly efficiently be converted into airline miles. You can transfer your rewards to dozens of different airline programs, and a vast majority allow a 3:1 transfer ratio. On top of that, you get a bonus of 5,000 airline miles for every 60,000 Bonvoy points you transfer. In other words, with most programs you can convert 60,000 Bonvoy points into 25,000 airline miles, which is potentially a decent value.

For more details, see my guide to redeeming Bonvoy points.

One of the primary reasons to consider getting the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless Card is how the card can help you earn elite status in the Bonvoy program. Status starts to get valuable around the Bonvoy Platinum tier, when you become eligible for perks like complimentary breakfast and valuable room upgrades.

One of my favorite perks of having the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless Card is that you get 15 elite nights toward status annually just for having the card.

Note that several co-branded Marriott credit cards offer this, and you can only receive the benefit once per year on a personal card. In other words, if you have three Marriott personal cards, then you wouldn’t get 45 elite nights.

However, you could earn 15 elite nights from this personal card and 15 elite nights from a business card, so that you’d earn 30 elite nights in a year. The ideal setup would be to have a personal card in conjunction with the Marriott Bonvoy Business® American Express® Card (learn more).

This makes it more attainable to earn Platinum status, which requires 50 elite nights. If you had the Bonvoy Boundless Card, you’d only need 35 more elite nights, and if you also had the business card you’d only need 20 more elite nights.

Note that if you really want to maximize elite nights with personal credit cards, the Marriott Bonvoy Brilliant® American Express® Card (learn more) offers 25 elite nights per year, which is the most elite nights you’ll get with any Marriott credit card.

The Marriott Bonvoy Boundless Card offers one elite night for every $5,000 spent on the card. Any elite nights earned this way will be credited to your account within eight weeks of the last day of the calendar month in which you qualify.

Personally, I think spending $5,000 to earn one elite night is a lot, but everyone’s situation will differ, and for some people, this could make sense if you’re otherwise close to earning status. This is the only Marriott credit card that offers bonus elite nights for spending.

Perhaps this is a bit redundant, but just for having the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless Card you receive Silver elite status in the Bonvoy program. Now, don’t get too excited, as this doesn’t exactly come with that many benefits.

Marriott Silver elite status ordinarily requires 10 elite nights, and comes with perks like 10% bonus points on hotel stays, priority late check-out, and free Wi-Fi. So it’s better than nothing, but that’s about all I can say.

If you have the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless Card, you can earn Marriott Gold elite status if you spend $35,000 on the card in a calendar year. This status ordinarily requires 25 elite nights. Bonvoy Gold elite status gets you benefits like 25% bonus points on hotel stays, 2PM late check-out, a room upgrade subject to availability, and more.

In addition to the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless Card spending bonus categories and ability to earn elite status, there are some other major perks to having the card. This is where the card’s annual fee becomes really easy to justify, in my opinion.

The real perk that makes the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless Card worthwhile is that you get a free night award every year on your account anniversary, valid for a one-night hotel stay at a property costing up to 35,000 points.

It’s also possible to top off Marriott free night awards with up to 25,000 additional points to redeem at more expensive properties. This means you could redeem a free night award plus 25,000 points to stay at a hotel costing 60,000 points per night.

This is an exceptional deal, and I think this card is worth having. Marriott is the world’s largest hotel chain, so regardless of your preferred hotel program, just about everyone may find themselves in a situation where this could come in handy.

I consistently redeem this certificate at hotels costing $250+ per night. Based on my valuation of 0.7 cents per point, I’d consider the free night award to be worth around $245, more than double the annual fee… that’s awesome!

The Marriott Bonvoy Boundless Card offers auto rental collision damage waiver coverage. Decline the rental company’s collision insurance and charge the entire rental cost to your card.

Coverage is provided for theft and collision damage for most cars in the United States and abroad. Do note that within the United States, coverage is secondary to your personal insurance, though. Of course you’ll always want to check the guide to benefits for all the details.

The Marriott Bonvoy Boundless Card offers a variety of protection when traveling. Among these features are:

Make sure you check your cardmember agreement and guide to benefits for all of the details, since there are terms to be aware of.

Personally, the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless Card isn’t a card that I would be using for my everyday spending. However, I think the card is worth having, given that it offers a free night certificate on your account anniversary every year, which should more than justify the annual fee.

If you’re going for status, the 15 elite nights toward status annually is incredibly valuable as well, and makes it easier to earn Platinum status.

I think there’s absolutely merit to picking up the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless Card, though I’d say that the Marriott Bonvoy Brilliant® American Express® Card (learn more) might be the best alternative to consider. While the card is issued by American Express and has a steep $650 annual fee (Rates & Fees), there are lots of reasons to consider this card, including:

Obviously this card won’t be for everyone, and the fee is steep. However, I do think the perks add up, and if you’re involved quite a bit in the Bonvoy ecosystem, it’s easy to make the math on the card work.

If you’re not actually that committed to the Marriott Bonvoy ecosystem, there are lots of other great cards to consider. In particular, these are cards with relatively reasonable annual fees and great rewards structures, and they’re very well rounded:

The Marriott Bonvoy Boundless Card is a great card with a reasonable annual fee, and offers an annual free night award and 15 elite nights toward status annually. This is an especially good time to apply, given the welcome offer that’s currently available.

For those looking to earn Bonvoy points, this is also one of Marriott’s better credit cards for being rewarded, between the points and additional elite nights. However, this still isn’t the card I’d be used for my everyday spending. Instead, this is a card you get for the perks it offers, as it can make sense to hold onto this card even with minimal spending.

#5972. Can You Redeem Airline Miles For Others? Yes, With Some Caveats

While I love redeeming miles & points for an amazing first or business class flight, one thing that brings me even more joy is being able to do that for friends & family. Along those lines, in this post I’d like to talk about which airline loyalty programs allow you to redeem your points for others. In a separate post, I addressed the topic of whether you can redeem hotel points for others.

While there are some areas where airline loyalty programs are stingy, the ability to redeem miles for others isn’t among those. Generally speaking, airline loyalty programs will let you redeem your miles for anyone you’d like (I’ll note some exceptions below, but unless otherwise noted, that’s what you should expect).

You can almost always do this directly through your frequent flyer program account, by just entering the name of the traveler during the booking process.

Now, it’s important to emphasize that this is for situations where you truly want to gift your rewards to others. Bartering airline miles violates the policies of virtually any airline loyalty program, and your account could be suspended and ticket could be forfeited if you’re caught doing this (and airline auditing departments are quite savvy).

So if you are going to redeem your airline miles for others, make sure you do so in good faith, without expecting anything in return.

To make things as easy as possible, I’d recommend that the person redeeming miles be the one to make the booking, rather than the person being redeemed for. Admittedly the policies do vary by airline:

If you’re making your reservation online, you can always just share your account number and password with someone to make a booking, though that does potentially pose a risk if you can’t fully trust the person (in which case you probably also shouldn’t share miles with them, come and think of it).

I won’t break that down by airline, since there are so many different policies, they sometimes change, and phone agents also often interpret them differently. However, the best way to go about this is to have the person with the miles make the booking. Just make sure you have the full, correct passport or travel document details for the traveler, so that the name matches the ID that will be presented at the time of travel.

There are hundreds of airline loyalty programs out there, and a vast majority of them will allow you to redeem your miles for anyone you’d like. There are some exceptions, though, as some airlines either limit the number of people you can redeem your miles for, or limit the types of people you can redeem your miles for (for example, direct family members).

Most of the programs restricting who you can redeem for are based in Asia. Let me note some of the most common programs with restrictions below. I’d like to emphasize, though, that this list is by no means exhaustive, so if I’ve missed any major programs, please do let me know.

Let me also mention that this is all about the program you book through, rather than the airline you travel with. For example, while All Nippon Airways Mileage Club has restrictions, you could book an award on All Nippon Airways through a partner program without being subjected to these rules.

There are airlines with just a few airplanes that have loyalty programs, so I’ll be focusing on “major” airlines, which I’ll define as airlines with 50+ planes. With that in mind, below are some of the major programs with restrictions:

With some programs that have these restrictions, you simply have to state what the relationship is between the person redeeming and the traveler. In other situations, you may have to provide proof of that relationship.

In some situations this gets tricky, like if we’re talking about same sex relationships that are recognized in some countries, but not others. For example, Korean Air SkyPass will accept same sex relationships as family if they’re recognized in a foreign country (and there’s documentation to prove it). However, since the South Korean government doesn’t legally recognize same sex relationships, a couple in the country wouldn’t be considered family for these purposes, unless they have a legally recognized relationship abroad.

With a vast majority of airline loyalty programs, you’re free to redeem your miles for friends & family without many restrictions. The best practice is to have the person redeeming the miles out of their account make the reservation.

There are a limited number of airline loyalty programs that limit who you can redeem your miles for. In some cases you’re limited to redeeming miles for direct family members, while in some cases you just have to specify redemption nominees, limiting the overall number of people you can redeem for.

What has your experience been with redeeming airline miles for others?

#5970. Finnair’s Cheap Avios Sale Offers A Shortcut To Status On American Flights And Access To Flagship Lounges

Finnair is selling 200,000 Avios for $2,170, and throwing in 20,000 points towards elite status. Those Avios can buy business class awards on Finnair, or move over to British Airways and Qatar Airways. And the status points can help you get into American Airlines Flagship lounges even when you’re flying domestic coach. The purchase alone gets you Finnair Silver, which is oneworld Ruby, and I don’t see much value in chasing Ruby. You get some airport priority on American and Alaska and a free checked bag. Finnair Gold, which is oneworld Sapphire, comes with lounge access including business class Flagship lounge access. The latest Frequent Miler on the Air episode walks through the sale and ways to leverage it. One Mile at a Time covered the offer when it launched. I’ve written about buying Finnair points to earn oneworld status since November 2020, and covered another version in December 2021. Those offers could get you all the way to Sapphire or Emerald without flying. This one is less generous for status, but the redeemable points are much more useful now that Finnair uses Avios than they were back then. What The Avios Cost Now The sale runs through November 16, 2026, ending at 4:59 p.m. Eastern. You need to have joined Finnair Plus before October 30 and have at least 50 Avios in your account. The purchase allowance has been reset for this offer: you can buy up to 200,000 even if you already hit the normal annual limit. The discount reaches 50% at 85,000 Avios. The best dollar pricing is available on purchases of 100,000 or more: 1.085 cents per Avios, before card rewards or shopping portal earnings. The purchase also generates tier points equal to 10% of the Avios bought. The podcast described paying in Japanese yen for about 1.06 cents apiece, then earning 3 points per dollar on an Atmos Rewards Summit card’s foreign purchases category. That yen price is no longer available and dollars are now the better deal. Purchases are processed by Points.com, not as airline tickets. Use a card with a strong return on otherwise unbonused spending. Finnair’s milestone rewards add another layer of benefits. A Basic member crossing 12,000 tier points receives 3,000 extra Avios. Starting at zero, and assuming that milestone hasn’t already been earned: Purchase Dollar Cost Avios Including Milestone Tier Points 120,000 Avios $1,302 123,000 12,000 150,000 Avios $1,627.50 153,000 15,000 200,000 Avios $2,170 203,000 20,000 The 120,000-point purchase works out to about 1.059 cents per Avios after the milestone. That’s slightly cheaper per point than buying the maximum. Existing Gold members don’t receive this Basic-tier milestone (Finnair only awards milestones within your own tier). Frequent Miler also flagged Rove at 1 mile per dollar and Extrabux at 1.6%–2% cash back as potential shopping portal optins to start with when buying the points. $1,302 would earn 1,302 Rove miles, which are also transferable to Finnair. Ruby Isn’t The Status I’d Spend Money Chasing Silver requires 15,000 tier points (not 20,000 as some discussions suggest, which is actually a separate milestone awarding two Finnair lounge passes). Buying 150,000 Avios already earns Silver from zero. Ruby gets you business class check-in and some seating and waitlist benefits. On American, it also means a free first checked bag and Group 4 boarding. Finnair Gold gives you oneworld business class lounge access, along with additional baggage and priority services. And because the status comes from Finnair rather than American or Alaska, American permits Flagship lounge access on eligible domestic trips as well. You can bring one guest. It doesn’t include Flagship Dining. You also get Admirals Club access and Alaska Lounge access when flying either airline. Gold also comes with four Finnair upgrade benefits covering one short-haul economy-to-business upgrade each or U.S.–Helsinki would use all four, requiring upgrade availability. You can also exchange all four for a two-for-one Finnair Classic economy or premium economy award. How To Get From This Sale To Sapphire Finnair Gold requires 45,000 tier points. Starting from zero, buying the maximum gives you 20,000. You can then exchange 22,500 Avios for 7,500 tier points. That leaves you with 27,500 tier points, 17,500 short of Gold, and 180,500 redeemable Avios if you received the Basic milestone. Finnair allows one exchange per personal tracking period, at three Avios per tier point, with a 500-tier-point minimum and a €10 online fee. The ceiling depends on your status when you exchange: 7,500 tier points for Basic or Silver, 22,500 for Gold, and 40,000 for Platinum or Platinum Lumo. An existing Gold member has a much easier renewal calculation. Buying 200,000 Avios generates 20,000 tier points, and converting 67,500 Avios adds 22,500. That’s 42,500 towards the 45,000 needed, leaving just 2,500 to earn if you started the period at zero. You’d retain 132,500 purchased Avios. For someone starting without status, American flights can fill the 17,500-point gap. Finnair’s earning chart for business class, including domestic flights with Finnair Silver status: J, C and D earn 250% of distance before the Silver bonus, or 275% with it. You’d need about 6,364 flown miles to generate 17,500 tier points. R and I earn 150%, or 165% with the Silver bonus. You’d need about 10,607 flown miles. Check your account’s personal tracking period before doing any of this. It isn’t the calendar year, and buying points or reaching Silver doesn’t restart it. Purchase, conversion and remaining flight credit need to fall in the same period. Once you reach Gold, the status lasts for the rest of that period plus the following 12 months. You Can Use Credit Card Points For The Final Top-Up You don’t have to buy Avios to use the conversion feature. If you’re 3,000 tier points short of Gold, you can transfer in 9,000 Avios and exchange them, paying the €10 online fee. Capital One transfers directly to Finnair at 1:1. Or transfer a bank currency into British Airways, then move those Avios into Finnair. Qatar Avios can go through British Airways to reach Finnair, too. Finnair’s current linking rules require an account at least 30 days old, matching names and email addresses, and two-factor authentication. That’s important even for getting the 50 Avios needed for the sale since an account opened shortly before the October 30 cutoff may qualify for the promotion but still be too new for an Avios-program transfer. The Avios You’re Buying Are Valuable, Too I covered Finnair’s improved award opportunities in May 2024. You can redeem through Finnair or move Avios 1:1, without a transfer fee, to British Airways and onward to Qatar or other Avios programs as well. Use a card with a strong return on otherwise unbonused spending.

Finnair’s milestone rewards add another layer of benefits. A Basic member crossing 12,000 tier points receives 3,000 extra Avios. Starting at zero, and assuming that milestone hasn’t already been earned:

The 120,000-point purchase works out to about 1.059 cents per Avios after the milestone. That’s slightly cheaper per point than buying the maximum. Existing Gold members don’t receive this Basic-tier milestone (Finnair only awards milestones within your own tier).

Frequent Miler also flagged Rove at 1 mile per dollar and Extrabux at 1.6%–2% cash back as potential shopping portal optins to start with when buying the points. $1,302 would earn 1,302 Rove miles, which are also transferable to Finnair.

Silver requires 15,000 tier points (not 20,000 as some discussions suggest, which is actually a separate milestone awarding two Finnair lounge passes). Buying 150,000 Avios already earns Silver from zero. Ruby gets you business class check-in and some seating and waitlist benefits. On American, it also means a free first checked bag and Group 4 boarding. Finnair Gold gives you oneworld business class lounge access, along with additional baggage and priority services. And because the status comes from Finnair rather than American or Alaska, American permits Flagship lounge access on eligible domestic trips as well. You can bring one guest. It doesn’t include Flagship Dining. You also get Admirals Club access and Alaska Lounge access when flying either airline. Gold also comes with four Finnair upgrade benefits covering one short-haul economy-to-business upgrade each or U.S.–Helsinki would use all four, requiring upgrade availability. You can also exchange all four for a two-for-one Finnair Classic economy or premium economy award. How To Get From This Sale To Sapphire Finnair Gold requires 45,000 tier points. Starting from zero, buying the maximum gives you 20,000. You can then exchange 22,500 Avios for 7,500 tier points. That leaves you with 27,500 tier points, 17,500 short of Gold, and 180,500 redeemable Avios if you received the Basic milestone. Finnair allows one exchange per personal tracking period, at three Avios per tier point, with a 500-tier-point minimum and a €10 online fee. The ceiling depends on your status when you exchange: 7,500 tier points for Basic or Silver, 22,500 for Gold, and 40,000 for Platinum or Platinum Lumo. An existing Gold member has a much easier renewal calculation. Buying 200,000 Avios generates 20,000 tier points, and converting 67,500 Avios adds 22,500. That’s 42,500 towards the 45,000 needed, leaving just 2,500 to earn if you started the period at zero. You’d retain 132,500 purchased Avios. For someone starting without status, American flights can fill the 17,500-point gap. Finnair’s earning chart for business class, including domestic flights with Finnair Silver status: J, C and D earn 250% of distance before the Silver bonus, or 275% with it. You’d need about 6,364 flown miles to generate 17,500 tier points. R and I earn 150%, or 165% with the Silver bonus. You’d need about 10,607 flown miles. Check your account’s personal tracking period before doing any of this. It isn’t the calendar year, and buying points or reaching Silver doesn’t restart it. Purchase, conversion and remaining flight credit need to fall in the same period. Once you reach Gold, the status lasts for the rest of that period plus the following 12 months. You Can Use Credit Card Points For The Final Top-Up You don’t have to buy Avios to use the conversion feature. If you’re 3,000 tier points short of Gold, you can transfer in 9,000 Avios and exchange them, paying the €10 online fee. Capital One transfers directly to Finnair at 1:1. Or transfer a bank currency into British Airways, then move those Avios into Finnair. Qatar Avios can go through British Airways to reach Finnair, too. Finnair’s current linking rules require an account at least 30 days old, matching names and email addresses, and two-factor authentication. That’s important even for getting the 50 Avios needed for the sale since an account opened shortly before the October 30 cutoff may qualify for the promotion but still be too new for an Avios-program transfer. The Avios You’re Buying Are Valuable, Too I covered Finnair’s improved award opportunities in May 2024. You can redeem through Finnair or move Avios 1:1, without a transfer fee, to British Airways and onward to Qatar or other Avios programs as well. #5969. How To Combine World Of Hyatt Points Between Accounts For Free

The major hotel loyalty programs all have different policies when it comes to combining points between accounts belonging to different members. I’ve already covered the options and policies for Hilton Honors and Marriott Bonvoy, and in this post, I’d like to take a look at the policy of World of Hyatt.

The good news is that World of Hyatt recently introduced a new way to transfer points to others for free, and I’d argue the program now has among the most generous policies in the industry. Long story short, you can transfer or receive up to 525,000 points per year, and this can all be done online, and at no cost. In this post, I’d like to look more closely at the mechanics of Hyatt points transfers.

World of Hyatt offers a generous feature to allow members to transfer points to others at no cost. Let’s first cover the basic rules for Hyatt points transfers:

It’s worth noting that this system is much better than it used to be. Back in the day combining Hyatt points required completing a form and took days, and you could only combine points in order to have sufficient points for a specific redemption. That policy no longer applies.

The process of transferring World of Hyatt points between members online is straightforward. To start, you can either follow this link, or go to your account overview page, and go to the section that reads “Gift your points more seamlessly.”

On the next page, you’ll want to go to the “Gift points or eligible awards” section, and then click “Gift your points.”

There you’ll first want to select how many points you want to transfer, using the slider.

Then on the next page, you’ll need to enter the account information for the account you want to move points to.

Then you’ll just need to confirm the details, and that’s it! Regarding transfer times, reports suggest transfers take anywhere from a few minutes to several days. It does seem like the more points you transfer, the more likely that it takes days for the transfer to go through. So if you are moving a large chunk of points, don’t be surprised if it takes some time.

What are the benefits to being able to combine points between World of Hyatt accounts? On the most basic level, it allows you to combine points so you have enough for an award stay. In other words, if you have two accounts with 15,000 points each, you can combine the points so you have enough for a one night stay at a hotel costing 30,000 points.

Furthermore, if you’re traveling as multiple people and one person has elite status, there’s value to booking the stay out of their account, so that you could take advantage of World of Hyatt Globalist or World of Hyatt Explorist benefits, for example.

However, thanks to the Guest of Honor program, it’s actually pretty easy to give elite perks to friends and family nowadays. For that matter, even Suite Upgrade Awards and Club Access Awards are transferable nowadays.

Lastly, combining points is also considered “activity” for the purposes of keeping your account alive, so it would reset the expiration of points.

World of Hyatt has a great system for letting members combine and share points. World of Hyatt members can transfer up to 525,000 points per year to other members, with limited restrictions. This is possible online, and typically points transfers happen pretty quickly.

There’s lots of value to this, and I’d say Hyatt’s policy is comparable to Hilton Honors for being the best in the industry.

If you’ve ever combined World of Hyatt points, what was your experience like?

#5964. Which Airlines Fly To The Most Destinations? Some May Surprise You

Recently, I wrote a post about the airlines that fly to the most countries. Turkish Airlines wins that title by a long shot, and has a 30+ country lead over the second most “global” airline.

In this post, I want to address a different but related topic — which airlines serve the most destinations? As you’d expect, this is a very different list. That’s because serving a lot of countries is much easier if you’re an airline that has a lot of service in Europe and Africa, given the number of countries there that are in close proximity. It’s one of the reason that US airlines don’t score that well when it comes to absolute number of countries served, despite otherwise being among the biggest carriers in the world.

However, the list of total number of destinations served is a different story…

I don’t think anyone will be surprised by the three airlines that serve the most destinations. As it currently stands:

This makes sense. In terms of fleets, the “big three” US carriers are among the biggest in the world. A majority of their networks are domestic, which is why the airlines don’t rank that high when it comes to total number of countries served, but they do great when it comes to the total number of destinations served. Note that the number of destinations also includes flights operated by their regional subsidiaries.

I don’t think the order above will surprise anyone. United is of course the most global US airline, and has a very impressive route network, including with ultra long haul flights. Meanwhile American is a massive domestic airline, and has a strong network in Latin America and the Caribbean, which is why it doesn’t appear that far behind United in terms of international destinations. And Delta, ummm, gets a revenue premium.

Just in the interest of being thorough, I’m sure some people are curious how many destinations Southwest serves, since it’s an absolutely massive airline in the United States, though doesn’t operate long haul flights. That number is less impressive — it’s a total of 120 destinations, including 104 domestic destinations and 16 international destinations. That’s because the airline is more about depth of service than breadth of service, and doesn’t have a regional subsidiary.

After US carriers, which airlines otherwise top the list of most destinations served? Most people wouldn’t be surprised to learn that Turkish takes that spot, serving 269 destinations, including 46 domestic destinations and 223 international destinations.

What about after that? Here are the next eight airlines (I think this is where some of the airlines may surprise people):

It’s interesting just how different the airlines on the list are. You have the “big three” Chinese carriers, the “big three” European carriers, and then you have Ryanair and Air Canada.

When you put it all together, below is the chart with the 12 airlines serving the most total destinations.

In the interest of being thorough, for those curious about Gulf carriers, Qatar Airways is in first place among them, serving 175 destinations, so it doesn’t quite make the list. Meanwhile Ethiopian Airlines, as Africa’s most global airline, serves 163 destinations

While Turkish Airlines flies to the most countries of any airline in the world, it doesn’t serve the most destinations. Instead that title goes to United, with the “big three” US carriers taking the three top spots. Then Turkish is in fourth place, and is followed by the “big three” Chinese carriers, the “big three” European carriers, and then also Ryanair and Air Canada.

Are you surprised by any of the airlines serving the most destinations?

#5963. American Airlines Updates Vouchers For Stranded Passengers—But Tells Employees There May Be Fewer Hotel Choices

American Airlines is updating how stranded passengers get hotel rooms, meal credits and rides during flight disruptions. An internal November memo I reviewed lays out automatic offers for eligible overnight delays and a new way for agents to arrange Uber rides without making passengers download the app. It also warns that employees may see fewer hotels to choose from. Getting passengers out of the customer service line and into a room sooner is great for getting sleep. On a recent American Airlines flight from New York to Austin that was cancelled after a long delay I didn’t even bother getting into the long line at the gate for a room voucher, I just booked something myself nad went on my way. What American Is Changing The update covers American’s Hotel, Meal and Transportation system, which employees call HMT. October 26: standalone meal credits. Agents can issue food and beverage credits for individual reservations affected by qualifying delays, cancellations and missed connections. The system uses flight information to evaluate eligibility and tells agents what qualifies. October 27: automatic offers for eligible overnight delays. The system sends hotel offers and applicable food and beverage credits when its eligibility and automation criteria are met, reducing the need for an employee to initiate the offer. Planned Uber Central rollout. At participating airports, authorized agents would arrange a ride on the customer’s behalf through the same system. The passenger receives a text message or WhatsApp link to start the ride, without downloading Uber. This should now be available but I haven’t seen passenger reports of the broadly available rollout yet (though customers reported it in limited release previously). Hotel inventory changes, date undetermined. American is changing the hotel inventory feed and selection process. Employees are told they may see fewer hotel choices. Automatic Vouchers Already Exist American has been working on this for years. I covered the electronic hotel and meal system in 2019, when agents still had to qualify customers and trigger offers. American was already describing automatic hotel, meal and transportation vouchers in 2025. This spring, they added meal issuance for an entire flight at once. In June, automatic meal vouchers expanded beyond elite members to all AAdvantage members. American’s January app changes already brought disruption assistance together: Their published customer service plan promises, upon request, an approved hotel for an overnight disruption they cause away from your city of residence, transportation there and back, and a food and beverage credit after a qualifying delay of at least three hours. The standard meal voucher I’ve been covering is $12. American recently renamed it a “food/beverage credit” because calling it a meal voucher led passengers to expect it to pay for a meal. How The Uber Change Works American already offers Uber vouchers. The change lets an agent arrange the ride for the passenger. Uber Central supports rides paid for by the business, with trip details sent to the customer. However, American’s instructions still put the hotel shuttle first, followed by an Uber voucher. Uber Central is for exceptions when those options don’t meet the customer’s needs. One passenger reported being at Washington National when agents refused Uber vouchers because a hotel had a shuttle even though it wasn’t running at 1 a.m. Fewer Hotel Choices Isn’t Great The memo’s most concerning sentence is: Frontline teams may see fewer hotel choices displayed than they are accustomed to seeing. Being able to choose a hotel matters. I’ve covered passenger complaints about unsuitable rooms and missing shuttles. Here’s a passenger who said the hotel floor was so dirty they spread sheets over it. If American can’t provide an approved hotel voucher, its customer service plan promises reimbursement of reasonable hotel costs. Its conditions of carriage also say reimbursement isn’t guaranteed when you book directly without written authorization. Credit card trip protections may reimburse required hotel overnights as well.
